sections.title: The JFET
sections.summary: Junction Field-Effect Transistor structure (n-channel and p-channel), schematic symbols, and the basic idea of a unipolar, voltage-controlled device whose gate-to-source pn junction is held in reverse bias.

sections.title: JFET Characteristics and Parameters
sections.summary: Drain characteristic curves, IDSS, pinch-off voltage VP, cutoff voltage VGS(off) (equal in magnitude but opposite polarity to VP), the square-law transfer equation ID = IDSS(1 − VGS/VGS(off))², transconductance gm = gm0(1 − VGS/VGS(off)) with gm0 = 2·IDSS/|VGS(off)|, input resistance from IGSS, and gate input capacitance.

sections.title: JFET Biasing
sections.summary: Self-bias (RS sets VGS), voltage-divider bias, and current-source bias. Midpoint-bias rule of thumb: VGS ≈ VGS(off)/3.4, ID ≈ IDSS/2. In self-bias the gate sits at 0 V (ground through RG); the source rises to make VGS = −ID·RS for an n-channel.

sections.title: The Ohmic Region
sections.summary: Below pinch-off the JFET behaves as a voltage-controlled resistor. Drain-to-source resistance depends on VGS, the Q-point values, and the slope of the curve at the Q-point. When biased at the origin (VDS ≈ 0, VGS = 0) the ac channel resistance is rds = 1/gm0, set entirely by the transconductance.

sections.title: The MOSFET
sections.summary: Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor FET — gate is insulated by a thin SiO₂ layer (no pn junction). The D-MOSFET has a physical channel and operates in BOTH depletion and enhancement modes. The E-MOSFET has no physical channel; a channel is induced only after VGS exceeds the threshold VGS(th) (enhancement mode only).

sections.title: MOSFET Characteristics and Parameters
sections.summary: Handling precautions for MOS devices (sensitive to electrostatic discharge — ESD), extremely high gate input resistance, RDS(on) which sets conduction power loss (P = ID²·RDS(on)), and the safe operating area (SOA) plotted on ID versus VDS.

sections.title: MOSFET Biasing
sections.summary: Zero-bias is natural for D-MOSFETs (at VGS = 0, ID = IDSS). E-MOSFETs require VGS beyond VGS(th) and use voltage-divider bias or drain-feedback bias to set the Q-point in the active region.

sections.title: The IGBT
sections.summary: The Insulated-Gate Bipolar Transistor combines a MOSFET-style insulated-gate input with a BJT-style high-current output. It is the device of choice for high-voltage, high-current switching: motor drives, inverters, and switched-mode power supplies.

sections.title: Troubleshooting
sections.summary: Common FET-circuit fault modes — opens and shorts in source, drain, and gate paths — and the dc-voltage signatures used to localize them.

questions.text: The JFET always operates with a reverse-biased gate-to-source pn junction.
questions.explanation: Reverse-biasing the gate-to-source junction is exactly what creates the depletion region that pinches the channel and gives the JFET its very high input impedance. Forward-biasing it would let gate current flow and destroy normal JFET behavior.

questions.text: The channel resistance of a JFET is a constant.
questions.explanation: The channel is narrowed by the depletion region, which grows or shrinks with VGS. As VGS becomes more negative (n-channel), the channel narrows and resistance rises — that's exactly how a JFET works as a voltage-controlled resistor in the ohmic region.

questions.text: The gate-to-source voltage of an n-channel JFET must be negative.
questions.explanation: For an n-channel JFET, VGS must be ≤ 0 to keep the gate-source pn junction reverse-biased. A positive VGS would forward-bias the junction and drive gate current, breaking JFET operation. (VGS = 0 is the limiting case that gives the maximum drain current IDSS.)

questions.text: ID becomes zero at the pinch-off voltage.
questions.explanation: At the pinch-off voltage VP, ID becomes CONSTANT (saturated at IDSS for VGS = 0), not zero. ID = 0 occurs at the cutoff voltage VGS(off), which is a different parameter. Don't confuse VP (on the drain curves) with VGS(off) (on the transfer curve).

questions.text: VGS has no effect on ID.
questions.explanation: VGS is the controlling variable for the JFET — it is precisely what determines ID through the square-law relation ID = IDSS(1 − VGS/VGS(off))².

questions.text: VGS(off) and VP are always equal in magnitude but opposite in polarity.
questions.explanation: VP (pinch-off voltage, defined on the drain curves at VGS = 0) and VGS(off) (cutoff voltage on the transfer curve) have the same magnitude but opposite signs. For an n-channel JFET with VP = +4 V, VGS(off) = −4 V.

questions.text: The JFET is a square-law device because of the mathematical expression of its transfer characteristic curve.
questions.explanation: The transfer relation ID = IDSS(1 − VGS/VGS(off))² is a square (parabolic) law — that's literally where the name 'square-law device' comes from.

questions.text: Forward transconductance is the change in drain voltage for a given change in gate voltage.
questions.explanation: Forward transconductance is the change in drain CURRENT for a given change in gate voltage: gm = ΔID/ΔVGS (units: siemens). The statement confuses voltage and current.

questions.text: The parameters gm and yfs are the same.
questions.explanation: Both symbols refer to the forward transfer admittance — the same physical quantity. gm is common in textbooks; yfs is the formal datasheet name.

questions.text: The D-MOSFET can be operated in two modes.
questions.explanation: The D-MOSFET (depletion MOSFET) has a physical channel and so works in BOTH depletion mode (VGS < 0 for n-channel, narrowing the channel) and enhancement mode (VGS > 0, widening it). That two-mode capability is its defining feature.

questions.text: An E-MOSFET operates in the depletion mode.
questions.explanation: The E-MOSFET has no physical channel; a channel must be INDUCED by VGS exceeding the threshold VGS(th). It operates only in the enhancement mode.

questions.text: A D-MOSFET has a physical channel and an E-MOSFET has an induced channel.
questions.explanation: Exactly the structural distinction between the two MOSFET families: the D-MOSFET is fabricated with a permanent doped channel; the E-MOSFET only has a channel after VGS pulls one into existence.

questions.text: ESD means electronic semiconductor device.
questions.explanation: ESD stands for Electrostatic Discharge — the static-electricity events that can puncture the very thin gate oxide of a MOSFET and destroy it.

questions.text: MOSFETs must be handled with care.
questions.explanation: Because of their susceptibility to ESD, MOSFETs are shipped with shorting clips or conductive foam, handled at grounded workstations, and worked on with antistatic wrist straps.

questions.text: The RDS(on) specification for a MOSFET determines the power and heating loss.
questions.explanation: When the MOSFET is fully on, conduction loss is PD = ID²·RDS(on). A lower RDS(on) means less heat for the same drain current — a key figure of merit for power MOSFETs.

questions.text: The safe operating area for a MOSFET can be shown on a graph of drain current versus gate voltage.
questions.explanation: The Safe Operating Area (SOA) is plotted as drain current ID versus drain-to-source voltage VDS, bounded by the maximum continuous current, the breakdown voltage, and the maximum power dissipation hyperbola. Not VGS.

questions.text: The JFET is
questions.explanation: The JFET is unipolar (only one carrier type — electrons in n-channel, holes in p-channel) AND voltage-controlled (VGS sets ID through a high-impedance reverse-biased gate). It is NOT current-controlled — that's a BJT.

questions.text: The channel of a JFET is between the
questions.explanation: The conducting channel runs from the source to the drain. The gate is the control terminal alongside the channel — it doesn't carry the channel current.

questions.text: A JFET always operates with
options: the gate connected to the source
questions.explanation: Reverse-biasing the gate junction is what gives the JFET its high input impedance and creates the depletion region used to control the channel.

questions.text: For VGS = 0 V, the drain current becomes constant when VDS exceeds
questions.explanation: At VGS = 0 V, increasing VDS past the pinch-off voltage VP puts the JFET in the constant-current region; ID then levels off at IDSS until breakdown.

questions.text: The constant-current region of a JFET lies between
questions.explanation: Below VP the JFET is in the ohmic region (ID rises with VDS). Above VP and below the breakdown voltage, ID is essentially flat — that flat band is the constant-current (active) region used for amplification.

questions.text: IDSS is
options: the drain current with the source shorted
questions.explanation: IDSS = Drain-to-Source current with the gate Shorted to source (VGS = 0). It's the maximum drain current the JFET will produce in normal operation; biasing the gate negative can only reduce ID below IDSS.

questions.text: Drain current in the constant-current region increases when
questions.explanation: In the constant-current region, ID is essentially independent of VDS but depends on VGS. As the magnitude of the (reverse) gate bias decreases — i.e., VGS moves toward 0 V — the depletion region narrows, the channel widens, and ID rises (toward IDSS).

questions.text: In a certain JFET circuit, VGS = 0 V, VDD = 15 V, IDSS = 15 mA, and RD = 470 Ω. If RD is decreased to 330 Ω, IDSS is
questions.explanation: IDSS is a JFET PARAMETER — the drain current at VGS = 0 in the constant-current region, set by the device itself, not by the external resistor. Changing RD does not change IDSS; the spec stays at 15 mA. (RD changes the load line, but not the device's IDSS rating.)

questions.text: At cutoff, the JFET channel is
options: completely closed by the depletion region
questions.explanation: At VGS = VGS(off), the depletion regions from each side of the channel meet and pinch the channel completely shut, so ID = 0.

questions.text: A certain JFET datasheet gives VGS(off) = −4 V. The pinch-off voltage, VP,
questions.explanation: VP and VGS(off) are equal in magnitude but opposite in polarity. With VGS(off) = −4 V → VP = +4 V.

questions.text: The JFET in Question 10 (with VGS(off) = −4 V)
questions.explanation: VGS(off) is NEGATIVE for an n-channel JFET (the gate must go negative to pinch the n-channel off) and POSITIVE for a p-channel. VGS(off) = −4 V → n-channel.

questions.text: For a certain JFET, IGSS = 10 nA at VGS = 10 V. The input resistance is
questions.explanation: RIN = VGS / IGSS = 10 V / 10 nA = 10 V / (10 × 10⁻⁹ A) = 1 × 10⁹ Ω = 1000 MΩ. (Note: your printed quiz seems to have a typo with both (c) and (d) reading '1000 MV'; the textbook (d) is 10,000 MΩ. Either way the answer is (c) 1000 MΩ.)

questions.text: In a certain JFET, IDSS = 5 mA and VGS(off) = −4 V. The value of gm0 is
questions.explanation: gm0 = 2·IDSS / |VGS(off)| = 2(5 mA) / 4 V = 10 mA / 4 V = 2.5 mS. (gm0 is the transconductance at VGS = 0; it's the maximum value of gm for that JFET.)

questions.text: For a certain p-channel JFET, VGS(off) = 8 V. The value of VGS for an approximate midpoint bias is
questions.explanation: Midpoint-bias rule of thumb: VGS ≈ VGS(off) / 3.4 = 8 V / 3.4 ≈ 2.35 V. (For a p-channel device, VGS(off) is positive, so the bias voltage is also positive — about +2.34 V — which gives ID ≈ IDSS/2.)

questions.text: In a self-biased JFET, the gate is at
questions.explanation: In a self-bias circuit the gate is tied to ground through RG. Because IGSS is essentially zero, no DC drop appears across RG, so VG = 0 V. The required negative VGS is produced by the source rising above ground (VS = ID·RS), giving VGS = VG − VS = −ID·RS. (Option (d) 'ground' describes the same node, but the textbook answer for the gate VOLTAGE is 0 V.)

questions.text: The drain-to-source resistance in the ohmic region depends on
options: the slope of the curve at the Q-point
questions.explanation: RDS in the ohmic region is set by VGS (which determines the channel width), by the Q-point (the operating values of ID and VDS), and equivalently by the slope of the drain curve at that Q-point — all three descriptions point to the same physical fact, so 'all of these' is correct.

questions.text: To be used as a variable resistor, a JFET must be
questions.explanation: Below pinch-off (the ohmic region), the JFET's drain curves are nearly linear through the origin and their slope — the channel resistance — varies with VGS. Either polarity of JFET works; the key requirement is operating below VP.

questions.text: When a JFET is biased at the origin, the ac channel resistance is determined by
questions.explanation: At the origin (VDS = 0, VGS = 0), the channel resistance reduces to rds = 1/gm0, so the transconductance alone fixes it. (Away from the origin, VGS and the Q-point both matter — but right at the origin, gm0 is the controlling parameter.)

questions.text: A MOSFET differs from a JFET mainly because
options: the JFET has a pn junction
MOSFETs do not have a physical channel
questions.explanation: The defining structural difference is the gate. The JFET uses a reverse-biased pn junction as its gate; the MOSFET uses a metal/poly gate insulated from the channel by a thin SiO₂ layer — no pn junction at all. (Note: D-MOSFETs DO have a physical channel, so option (d) is wrong — only E-MOSFETs lack one.)

questions.text: A D-MOSFET operates in
options: both the depletion and enhancement modes
questions.explanation: Because the D-MOSFET has a physical channel, applying VGS of either sign works: negative VGS depletes the channel (depletion mode) and positive VGS enhances it (enhancement mode).

questions.text: An n-channel D-MOSFET with a positive VGS is operating in
questions.explanation: Positive VGS on an n-channel D-MOSFET pulls more electrons into the channel, widening it and increasing ID above IDSS — that's enhancement-mode operation.

questions.text: A certain p-channel E-MOSFET has a VGS(th) = −2 V. If VGS = 0 V, the drain current is
questions.explanation: An E-MOSFET only conducts when VGS is past the threshold. A p-channel device needs VGS more NEGATIVE than VGS(th) = −2 V (e.g., −3 V) to turn on. At VGS = 0 V, the device is OFF and ID = 0. (IDSS is a JFET / D-MOSFET parameter — it doesn't apply to E-MOSFETs at all.)

questions.text: In an E-MOSFET, there is no drain current until VGS
questions.explanation: VGS(th) is the threshold voltage at which the channel is just induced. Below threshold the E-MOSFET is off. The required polarity of VGS(th) depends on whether the device is n- or p-channel — so 'positive' or 'negative' alone is incomplete.

questions.text: All MOS devices are subject to damage from
questions.explanation: MOS devices can be damaged by all three: heat (junction temperature exceeding the rated maximum), ESD (puncturing the thin gate oxide), and excessive voltage (breakdown of gate oxide or drain-source). ESD is the most distinctive MOSFET failure mode, but the other two apply too.

questions.text: A certain D-MOSFET is biased at VGS = 0 V. Its datasheet specifies IDSS = 20 mA and VGS(off) = −5 V. The value of the drain current
questions.explanation: For a D-MOSFET, IDSS is by definition the drain current at VGS = 0 V (the zero-bias point). So ID = IDSS = 20 mA. This is exactly why D-MOSFETs work so well with the ultra-simple zero-bias configuration — no source resistor required.

questions.text: An IGBT is generally used in
questions.explanation: The IGBT marries a MOSFET-style high-impedance gate with a BJT-style low-conduction-loss output. That combination makes it the dominant device for high-voltage, high-current switching: motor drives, traction inverters, welding equipment, and switched-mode power supplies.
